study_material.title: Data Interpretation - Complete Study Notes
study_material.introduction: DI presents data as tables, bar graphs, line graphs, pie charts or mixed diagrams and asks for totals, averages, percentages and ratios. The math is elementary - the skill is reading the right numbers fast and avoiding calculation traps.
learning_objectives: Read tables, bar/line graphs and pie charts accurately
Compute totals, averages, percentage changes and ratios from data
Convert pie-chart degrees to values and back
Approximate smartly to eliminate wrong options

concepts.heading: 1. Tables and Bar Graphs
concepts.body: Tables give exact values; bar graphs compare categories visually. Typical asks: total across years, average per category, percentage growth between two years, the year with maximum increase. Always note units (lakhs, crores, thousands).

concepts.heading: 2. Line Graphs
concepts.body: Best for trends over time. Percentage increase = (new - old)/old x 100 - the base is the earlier value. Steepest segment = largest absolute change; largest percentage change may differ because bases differ.

concepts.heading: 3. Pie Charts
concepts.body: The full circle is 360 degrees = 100% of the total. Value of a sector = (sector degrees/360) x total, or (sector %/100) x total. A 90-degree sector is 25%. To compare two sectors, their degree ratio equals their value ratio.

concepts.heading: 4. Mixed Diagrams and Caselets
concepts.body: Some sets combine a pie chart with a table, or give data in a paragraph (caselet). Extract the numbers into a quick table first, then answer. Half the errors in DI come from picking the wrong row or year.

concepts.heading: 5. Approximation
concepts.body: Options are usually far apart - round values to 2-3 significant digits before dividing. Compute percentages via convenient fractions: 12.5% = 1/8, 16.67% = 1/6, 33.33% = 1/3.

formulas: Ratio of sectors = ratio of degrees
shortcut_methods: Convert percentages to fractions before multiplying
Scan options first - precision needed depends on their spacing
In multi-year tables, mark the two cells you need before computing
common_mistakes: Using the new value as the base in percentage change
Missing units stated in the title or axis (lakhs vs crores)
Comparing absolute changes when percentage change is asked
Misreading adjacent rows or columns under time pressure
study_material.summary: Read the axes, note the units, pick the exact cells needed, and approximate with fraction equivalents - DI is accuracy plus speed, not advanced math.
